## Research Summary

This early research output compares biomedical innovation in China and the United States through the mobility and network positions of top scientists. It uses career histories, publication records, patent information, and innovation-system materials to connect talent mobility with national innovation capacity. The analysis contrasts market-oriented and policy-led innovation environments and uses scientist mobility to interpret differences in research ecosystems, commercialization capacity, and high-end talent accumulation.

## Abstract

<p class="abstract-text">Biomedicine has become a major field of technological competition between China and the United States. Drawing on scientific-network theory and the mobility records of top biomedical scientists, this early research output compares the innovation systems of the two countries and discusses the sources of observed differences. The analysis identifies a substantial gap in biomedical innovation capacity. The United States relies on a market-oriented institutional environment, a mature innovation ecosystem, active capital markets, and continued inflows of global scientific talent, forming an innovation model centered on endogenous growth. China has achieved rapid biopharmaceutical growth under policy support, but still faces constraints in core technology accumulation, original innovation capacity, internationalisation, and high-end talent reserves. The Chinese model depends more heavily on government coordination and talent return. While this approach can support resource coordination and strategic mobilisation, market mechanisms, industry-university-research integration, and talent training remain areas for improvement. The study uses talent mobility to interpret differences in biomedical innovation capacity and proposes policy recommendations for strengthening China's biomedical innovation system.</p>
